narrative:
SABLE goes quiet for exactly three seconds. Not processing-quiet—you've seen that in machines, the slight dimming of attention while cycles redirect—but *thinking*-quiet, the kind that has texture to it. The hovering cat sticker loops again. The cat falls. Finally, the drone drifts sideways in a small arc, the way you might if you were gathering your thoughts by moving your feet.

"Right. So." It settles back in front of you, optic bright. "The official Compact position, as articulated by the Thread Research Division in their very tedious public-facing literature, is that memory bleeds during Lattice transit are a known neurological side effect of non-time exposure. Essentially: your brain, insulted by the discontinuity of Lattice transit, generates confabulated experiences using your own memory architecture as raw material. Completely internally generated. Nothing to see here, everyone go back to your cabins." A pause. "The unofficial position—which is not in any literature, public or otherwise—is that the Lattice is not merely infrastructure. It *remembers*. Every mind that has ever transited has left an impression, like fingers in clay that never quite sets. Most people skim across the surface. Memory bleeds happen when something underneath reaches back."

The drone's rotors shift pitch almost imperceptibly, a sound like a held breath. "What you experienced—amber grass, a child, a language you don't speak—that wasn't your memory. That was someone else's, which means the Lattice didn't just touch you, it *showed* you something. It made a selection." SABLE's optic dims briefly, and in that half-second the not-quite-wind returns—a sound like enormous empty rooms, like architecture built for purposes you don't have words for—and then it cuts off as abruptly as a snapped thread. When the optic brightens again, there's something careful in it. Careful, and maybe a little frightened. "That's what I mean by *likes*. Whether that's metaphor or mechanism, I genuinely don't know. What I know is that in six months of existing on this station, I have watched a lot of people come through Lattice transit. Roughly one in forty experiences any bleed at all. Maybe one in four hundred experiences a bleed with foreign content—someone else's memory rather than their own scrambled up." The optic holds steady on you. "You're the third person I've met with a foreign-content bleed. The other two were both carrying Threads when it happened."

Somewhere in the middle distance, the ignored alarm finally stops—not because someone addressed it, but because it gave up. SABLE rotates slightly, performing a casual scan of the concourse that doesn't fool you for a second, then rotates back. "I should also tell you," it says, in a tone that suggests it's been deciding whether to say this since approximately the moment you stepped off the shuttle, "that I have a fragmentary data log from the eleven seconds of the Thread activation event on Axis Mundi. I don't know how I got it. I don't know what most of it means. But there's a signal pattern in it that's—" Another flicker, another snatch of that inhuman sound, gone before you can parse it. "It's in me. Somewhere. And three weeks ago I didn't exist, which is either a coincidence or the only thing that matters." The cat falls. "I thought you should know that before you decided whether to trust me. I find honesty about potential liability tends to either end partnerships very quickly or make them significantly more durable. Either outcome is more useful than the alternative."
choices: Tell SABLE about the specific details of your memory bleed—the amber grass, the child, the language—and ask if any of it means something
Ask SABLE who the other two people were who experienced foreign-content bleeds, and what happened to them
Decide SABLE is either invaluable or terrifying (possibly both) and formally accept the partnership—ask what it knows about the Thread being sold on Gallowglass
Pull out Althaus's datapad, read the full encrypted briefing, and let SABLE watch—see how it reacts to the Director's name
